demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile unless she was also physically injured, which is not reflected elsewhere. The other selected appraisals center on self-blame and humiliation, which fit this trauma type, but this item introduces a different trauma meaning without supporting threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a broad, ongoing danger/vulnerability pattern focused on personal safety (restricted safe places, nighttime checking for safety). For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another person, this is hard to reconcile unless there is additional trauma involving danger to self; the threat content would more plausibly center on fear of causing harm again, moral threat, or social/legal consequences.

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active edge is Threat → Negative Appraisals, so threat and appraisals should show a plausible thematic link. Here the threat items center on physical safety and hypervigilance, while the appraisals center on guilt, self-blame, and humiliation about having caused harm. That disconnect suggests the selected threat items are not well aligned with the appraisals for this trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: For trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the threat profile is poorly matched: nocturnal checking for safety and inability to relax in safe places imply an ongoing danger/victimization-based fear response, but the appraisals center on guilt and self-blame about causing harm. That combination is hard to reconcile clinically without any items about fear of legal retaliation, being attacked, or another external threat.

issues.item: Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active link is Threat → Negative Appraisals, so threat items should plausibly feed the selected appraisals. Here the threat items suggest current physical danger/hypervigilance, whereas the negative appraisals are predominantly moral self-judgment and shame. Humiliation in particular is weakly connected to the stated threat content, making the cross-node pattern clinically incoherent.

vignette:
At 66, Diane had spent decades in front of cameras and under bright lights, and she still worked steadily enough as a commercial model to keep a regular schedule of castings, fittings, and long studio days. She was a widow and lived alone, and when she first described the event that brought her to treatment, she did so with the flat precision of someone who had replayed it too many times. Months earlier, she had been driving to a photo shoot when she was involved in an accident in which another person was seriously injured. In Diane's telling, the worst part was not only seeing the immediate aftermath but the unbearable conviction that there had been a moment, however small, when she should have done something differently. Her mind kept returning to the seconds before impact and to what followed, searching for the point at which she believed she failed. She had come to believe that a more competent person, a more alert person, simply would not have gotten into that situation. When she said this, it did not sound abstract or philosophical; it sounded like a verdict.

In the days after the accident, Diane found that her body no longer settled. Even sitting in her own living room with the television on low, she could feel herself held tight, shoulders raised, jaw set, as if bracing for something else to happen. She knew perfectly well that she was at home and safe, but the knowledge did not translate into ease. She described trying to relax on the sofa and realizing that her hands were clenched in her lap. She would notice the tension only because it had become painful. At night she would lie in bed waiting for her muscles to release and feel instead that her whole body was poised to react. The feeling was not tied to any one place. It followed her into ordinary moments that used to be neutral.

Her work made this especially visible. In the studio, where she had once moved easily through directions and quick changes, she began to struggle to hold her attention on simple tasks. A stylist would explain the order of looks, or a photographer would adjust her position, and Diane would catch herself drifting, unable to keep track of what had just been said. She found this deeply unsettling and embarrassing. Modeling had long depended on her ability to stay composed and responsive in fast-moving environments. Now, under the scrutiny of crews much younger than she was, she felt exposed by her own lapses. If someone repeated instructions, she heard it as confirmation that she was no longer reliable. She had become certain that other people could see the accident on her, not literally, but as a kind of stain. What frightened her was not only being judged for having caused serious harm to another person, but being seen as the sort of woman who could do such a thing.

That sense of humiliation hardened over time. Diane stopped chatting easily on set and kept interactions clipped and formal. She began arriving as late as she thought she could without being unprofessional, preferring less idle time in makeup chairs or green rooms where conversation might turn personal. She avoided questions about how she had been doing. If a job required prolonged downtime between setups, she would sit rigidly with a magazine open and absorb almost none of it, too tense to rest and too distracted to focus. Even among familiar people, she felt she had been reduced by what happened. She described it as permanent, as though the accident had fixed her in the eyes of others and in her own.

Alongside this, Diane remained preoccupied with what she had not done. She returned again and again to the belief that she should have done more to stop what happened, though when she tried to explain exactly what "more" meant, she could not arrive at anything that relieved her. The lack of relief seemed only to deepen her self-reproach. She spoke as if forgiveness were not merely difficult but prohibited. To forgive herself would, in her mind, be to minimize the seriousness of the injury and her responsibility for it.

By the time she sought help, these patterns had narrowed her life. Work, once a place where she felt practiced and at ease, had become another setting in which she monitored herself and came up wanting. At home she could not fully unwind, even in the quietest parts of the day. She noticed her concentration slipping in conversations, in reading, even in following a recipe, and each lapse seemed to confirm her harsh comparison between herself and the person she thought she should have been. She came to treatment after a recent job on which she lost track of repeated directions and then sat in the dressing area afterward, humiliated and trembling with tension, unable to calm herself before driving home. What she wanted most was not absolution so much as the possibility of getting through a day without feeling constantly braced and ashamed. What she feared most was that this was now her permanent self: the woman who caused irreversible harm and could never stop reliving her failure to prevent it.
